The Sixth Sense. M. Night Shyamalan's nineteen ninety-nine psychological thriller about a child psychologist treating a boy who claims to see dead people.

Haley Joel Osment plays Cole Sear, a withdrawn nine-year-old boy famous for whispering the film's most memorable line: I see dead people. Bruce Willis plays Doctor Malcolm Crowe, a renowned child psychologist who becomes Cole's mentor and confidant, helping him accept and understand his supernatural visions.

The film portrays Crowe as a successful, living professional treating a traumatized child. Their relationship appears to be genuine therapeutic progress. The boy's supernatural ability is gradually accepted by both Crowe and the audience, and the narrative shifts toward spiritual acceptance and healing. It is a story about a compassionate doctor helping a vulnerable child overcome his fears.

But in the final minutes, the film delivers its twist. Crowe is revealed to be a ghost. He was shot by a resentful former patient at the film's opening, a scene that the viewer witnesses and recontextualizes only in the twist's final moments as his death, not a random attack. Crowe's entire narrative role is revealed as a form of unconscious purgatory. He has been unable to leave behind his work or accept his death. Instead, he has constructed an elaborate false reality in which he continues his therapeutic practice.

Crowe's arc reverses from helper to subject needing help. Suddenly, Cole's own wounds mirror Crowe's unprocessed grief. The supernatural elements that seemed to drive the film's genre are revealed to have been operating on an entirely different level. Shyamalan became famous for high-concept twist endings, and the film's technical execution in editing, sound, and performance masterfully masks its supernatural reality from the viewer.
